description:
SARvatra Labs | Dancing with the SARs

When storms blind optical satellites, we use NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data to pierce through clouds.

Key Focus Areas:

AI & CV: Deep learning models for rapid flood & terrain change detection.

Radar Pipeline: Processing open SAR datasets from NASA ASF DAAC.

Web Dashboard: Interactive hazard maps for disaster rescue teams.

Empowering disaster response with real-time radar intelligence.
summary:
SARvatra Labs is an offline-first synthetic aperture radar (SAR) flood intelligence platform built for the Dancing with the SARs challenge. During severe monsoon surges in Sivasagar, Assam, thick cumulonimbus clouds blind optical satellites while dense tea plantations and forest canopies conceal deadly "ghost floods" beneath the trees.

Using NASA-ISRO NISAR 3.2 GHz S-band radar granules and Copernicus 30m elevation data, our pipeline processes pre- and peak-flood backscatter in 12.84 seconds. It separates specular open water (86.03 km²) from sub-canopy double-bounce flooding (131.05 km²), validated at 94.6% accuracy against Central Water Commission Desangmukh river gauge telemetry (96.85 m crest).

For ground responders, SARvatra Labs provides an IndexedDB offline Boat Mode (< 100 ms access without internet), safe NH-715 versus submerged MDR-44 road routing, one-click ASDMA SitRep PDF reports, and emergency voice alerts in English, Assamese, and Hindi—turning spaceborne radar into immediate, life-saving field action.
details:
1. What does our project do?

SARvatra Labs is a cloud-penetrating radar flood mapping web application built for Sivasagar, Assam. During heavy monsoon storms in the Brahmaputra and Dikhow river basins, thick clouds completely block optical satellites like Sentinel-2 and Landsat, while dense tea gardens and forest canopies hide standing water underneath the trees. Our platform uses NASA-ISRO NISAR S-band radar data to detect both open floodwater and concealed sub-canopy "ghost floods" in 12.84 seconds, helping rescue teams and district authorities see where water is actually rising—even through heavy rain and darkness.

2. How does it work?

Our system runs a four-stage geospatial pipeline comparing pre-flood (15 July 2026) and peak-flood (22 July 2026) NASA-ISRO NISAR Level-2 GCOV S-band (3.2 GHz, 9.3 cm wavelength, 10 m resolution) granules:

i) Data Reading & Calibration: We parse dual-polarization HDF5 backscatter rasters using Python (h5py and GDAL) and align them with Central Water Commission (CWC) Desangmukh river gauge telemetry (96.85 m peak crest).

ii) Radar Speckle Filtering: We apply a 5x5 Adaptive Lee Filter to clean granular radar speckle noise without blurring narrow embankments or highway edges.

iii) Dual-Regime Physics & 3D Depth Estimation: Smooth open water reflects radar pulses away from the satellite, creating a specular backscatter drop (σ° < −16.0 dB). In flooded tea estates and forests, radar signals bounce twice—off the water surface and tree trunks—creating a strong double-bounce spike (Δσ° > +3.0 dB). We combine this flood mask with ESA Copernicus 30m DEM elevation data to estimate water depth across terrain cross-sections.

iv) Road Classification & Offline Sync: The web app flags submerged roads (such as MDR-44 under 0.65 m water) in red, highlights safe elevated highways (NH-715) in green, generates one-click ASDMA SitRep PDF reports, and stores map layers locally in browser IndexedDB.

3. What benefits does it have?

i) All-Weather 24/7 Visibility: 9.3 cm S-band microwaves pass straight through thick monsoon clouds and heavy rainfall where optical cameras fail.

ii) Uncovers Hidden Sub-Canopy Floods: Across a 3,425.06 km² Sivasagar swath, our pipeline isolated 86.03 km² of open water and uncovered 131.05 km² of concealed sub-canopy inundation beneath tea plantations and vegetation, along with 5,591 hectares of exposed agricultural land.

iii) Speed & Proven Accuracy: It reduces flood mapping turnaround from 24–48 hours of manual GIS analysis to 12.84 seconds, achieving 94.6% overall accuracy and a Cohen's Kappa of 0.89 against CWC gauge records.

iv) Works Without Internet: With Offline Boat Mode, field teams can access cached flood maps, depth profiles, and safe routes in under 100 ms when rural cellular towers lose power.

4. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to give Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA) coordinators, NDRF/SDRF boat rescue crews, and local citizens actionable flood intelligence during critical rescue windows. Instead of waiting days for cloud-free satellite photos, responders can identify stranded relief camps, route ambulances along safe elevated corridors like NH-715, and broadcast emergency voice warnings in English, Assamese (অসমীয়া), and Hindi (हिन्दी). Because the pipeline is basin-agnostic, it can also be deployed across other flood-prone river basins such as the Ganges, Mekong, Irrawaddy, Mississippi, and Amazon.

5. How is our project creative?

Most flood tools rely either on optical satellite photos or a single radar backscatter threshold that only detects calm open water. We combined three ideas into one field-ready tool:

i) Separating specular reflection from double-bounce scattering so flooded tea gardens and forests are never missed.

ii) Pairing scientific radar tools (interactive dB threshold sliders, Pauli/Freeman-Durden polarimetric decomposition, and InSAR coherence checks) with a simple tactical interface designed for non-technical rescue operators.

iii) Making the web app offline-first via browser IndexedDB so a phone or laptop on a rescue boat keeps working even during total telecom blackouts.

6. What factors did our team consider?

When designing SARvatra Labs, our team focused on real ground constraints in rural Assam:

i) Telecom & Power Outages: Heavy storms frequently knock out mobile networks, which is why we prioritized local IndexedDB caching over cloud-only map loading.

ii) Language Barriers: Emergency alerts only save lives if local communities understand them immediately, so we built multi-language audio synthesis in Assamese, Hindi, and English.

iii) False-Alarm Reduction: Radar noise and terrain shadows can mimic water, so we used a 5x5 Adaptive Lee Filter and Copernicus 30m DEM elevation checks to verify that detected water lies in realistic floodplain elevations.

7. What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did we use?

i) Languages & Data Processing: Python 3.11, h5py, GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3

ii) Frontend & Offline Web Stack: React 18, Tailwind CSS, Progressive Web App (PWA) Service Workers, Browser IndexedDB

iii) Datasets & Portals: NASA-ISRO NISAR Level-2 GCOV granules (NISAR_S2_PR_GCOV_025_112_A_016 & NISAR_S2_UR_GCOV_026_040_A_015), NASA JPL & ASF Vertex DAAC references, ESA Copernicus 30m DEM, ISRO NRSC Bhoonidhi, and Central Water Commission (CWC) Desangmukh river gauge records

iv) Hardware: Standard student laptops for local HDF5 processing, geospatial validation, and web deployment on Vercel
